issues.legal_issue: A state that has transferred land to a local body subject to a continuing power of resumption retains a legal interest sufficient to seek its recovery from a trespasser.
material_facts: The estate first vested absolutely in the State after the abolition of intermediary rights.
The State later vested the disputed land in a village body, but retained statutory power to resume it and to control its management.
The former intermediary continued to claim and occupy the land, which included structures and open areas used for a cattle fair.
issues.conclusion: The State retained title sufficient to sustain the suit for ejectment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 6 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, estates initially vested absolutely in the State. Read with Sections 117(1) and 117(6), and the State’s control over local management under Sections 122A, 122B and 126, a later vesting in a village body is qualified: it gives possession and enjoyment subject to resumption. The word “vest” takes its meaning from its context, and treating the later vesting as absolute would undermine the resumption power in Section 117(6).

rule.if: suit_for_ejectment_on_title and estate_initially_vested_in_state and land_transferred_to_local_body_subject_to_resumption and trespasser_claimed_or_occupied_land

predicates.suit_for_ejectment_on_title: The proceeding sought recovery of land from an alleged trespasser on the basis of title.
predicates.estate_initially_vested_in_state: The estate first became the State’s property after the prior intermediary rights ended.
predicates.land_transferred_to_local_body_subject_t: The State later gave a local body possession or enjoyment of the land while retaining power to take it back.
predicates.trespasser_claimed_or_occupied_land: A person continued to claim or occupy the land despite the State’s interest in it.

issues.definition: When an estate first belongs to the State, is later placed with a local body subject to resumption, and is claimed or occupied by a trespasser, the State retains title to seek recovery in an ejectment suit.

issues.legal_issue: A public body with a genuine grievance arising from threatened harm to community property may appeal the dismissal of a civil suit even when its connection to the dispute is not purely personal.
material_facts: The State and a village body jointly brought a suit seeking relief against the former intermediary’s occupation of the estate.
The trial court dismissed the suit; the village body did not appeal, but the State did.
The State retained control over the local body’s management of the estate and could resume the land, while the alleged trespass threatened the public purpose for which the land had been vested.
issues.conclusion: The State was a person aggrieved and was entitled to appeal under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an appeal by a party aggrieved by a decree. The meaning of “person aggrieved” is not confined to a person whose personal or proprietary right has been directly violated; a genuine grievance that an order prejudicially affects an interest can suffice. The Court relied on Dhabolkar, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 306, and referred to Re Sidebotham and Attorney-General of the Gambia v. Peirra Sarr N'Jie in explaining the broader understanding of standing. A public body may pursue a wrong against community interest where its public responsibilities and continuing legal interest are threatened.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_dismissed_suit: A public body appealed the dismissal of a civil suit.
predicates.appeal_seeks_protection_of_community_pro: The appeal sought to protect property held or used for community benefit.
predicates.public_body_retains_legal_control_or_res: The public body continued to oversee the property or had power to recover it from the local body holding it.
predicates.threatened_loss_impairs_public_duty: The threatened loss of the property would obstruct the public body’s responsibility to protect or preserve it for public use.

issues.definition: A public body may appeal a dismissed civil suit as an aggrieved person when it seeks to protect community property over which it retains legal control and the threatened loss would impair its public duty.

issues.legal_issue: Land is appurtenant to a building only to the extent that it is subordinate or necessary to the use of the building as a building, not merely because it is used with the building for a separate activity.
material_facts: The estate contained buildings and structures associated with a cattle fair, as well as large open spaces used for the fair.
The former intermediary argued that the buildings and the entire fairground formed one functional whole.

The High Court allowed the former intermediary to retain the structures and five yards of surrounding space; the Supreme Court held that the larger open areas were not needed for use of the structures as buildings.
issues.conclusion: The large open spaces used for the cattle fair were not appurtenant to the buildings; the allowance of surrounding space for the structures was sound in law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, settles buildings and the sites appurtenant to them with the existing owner or occupier. Appurtenance implies subordination, dependence, or an incidental relationship to the principal subject. The touchstone is whether the building depends on the land for its use as a building; land used for a distinct activity does not become appurtenant merely because it was historically enjoyed together with the building. The Court also relied on the ordinary legal meaning of “appurtenance” described in Words and Phrases Legally Defined.

predicates.dispute_over_land_settled_with_buildings: The dispute concerns whether land is included with buildings under a settlement of property to an existing owner or occupier.
predicates.surrounding_land_serves_a_separate_activ: The surrounding land is used for an activity distinct from the use of the buildings themselves.
predicates.surrounding_land_is_not_needed_for_build: The buildings can be used as buildings without the surrounding land beyond what is reasonably needed for their use.

issues.definition: When land around buildings serves a separate activity and is not needed for the buildings’ use, it is not appurtenant to them.
